title: Advanced Solidity & Smart Contract Development
tagline: Storage and gas, design patterns, proxies and upgrades, signatures, advanced testing and production discipline
summary: An advanced, design-led course for developers who already write Solidity: storage layout and gas, state machines, pull payments, clones and roles, delegatecall and UUPS upgrades, signatures and EIP-712, fuzz and invariant testing, documentation, threat modelling and release practice. All Solidity listings were compiled with solc 0.8 against OpenZeppelin 5, and you run them yourself in your own tools.

modules.title: Storage, packing and gas
modules.summary: How the EVM lays out storage, what each operation costs and which optimisations are worth their risk.
modules.outcome: You can predict storage slots, pack variables, choose calldata and unchecked blocks wisely and measure the gas saved.
modules.intro: Gas is the currency of correctness on Ethereum: wasteful code costs users money every time it runs. But optimising too early produces code nobody can verify. This module teaches what to optimise, how to measure it and when to stop.

topics.title: How storage is laid out
topics.html:
Contract storage is an enormous array of 32-byte slots numbered from zero. State variables are assigned to slots in the order they are declared. Several small variables can share one slot, but only when they are neighbours and fit together. Reading or writing a slot is one of the most expensive things a contract does.

What happens
ContractLayoutSlots
Unpackeda (16 bytes) in slot 0, b (32 bytes) needs a whole slot so goes to slot 1, c (16 bytes) goes to slot 23
Packeda and c together in slot 0 (16 + 16 = 32 bytes), b in slot 12
Approximate storage costs
OperationGas (order of magnitude)
First access to a slot in a transaction ('cold')About 2,100 for a read
Writing zero to non-zeroAbout 22,100 including the cold access
Changing a non-zero value to anotherAbout 5,000
Setting non-zero to zeroCosts gas but earns a partial refund

Check what you just learned

1. Why does the Packed contract use fewer slots?
  • It uses fewer functions
  • The two uint128 values sit next to each other and share one slot (correct)
  • It has no events
  • It is a library

Order matters for packing.

Watch out

Packing helps only when the packed variables are read or written together. Mixing unrelated values into one slot can make each write more expensive because the EVM must read and mask the neighbours.

Check what you just learned

1. A new storage slot written for the first time costs roughly:
  • 21 gas
  • 2,100 gas
  • 22,100 gas (correct)
  • 1 million gas

It is by far the dearest common operation.
keyPoints: Storage is 32-byte slots assigned in declaration order.
Neighbouring small variables can share a slot; order matters.

topics.title: Cheaper code, safely
topics.html:
Techniques shown
TechniqueWhy it saves gasRisk
calldata instead of memoryNo copy of the arrayRead-only, so you cannot modify it
Cache the length in a local variableAvoids re-reading xs.lengthNone
unchecked { ++i; }Skips an overflow check that can never trigger for a loop counter bounded by the array lengthDangerous if the bound is not truly safe
Custom errorsCheaper than string messagesNone
constant and immutableNo storage readFixed at compile or deployment time
Short-circuit cheap checks firstFails early before expensive workNone

Loop gas, roughly

Change the number of items to see a teaching estimate of gas for the memory version (about 180 gas per item) and the calldata version with unchecked counter (about 120 gas per item). Measure real values with a gas report.

Adjust Items and see Memory version (rough gas), Calldata and unchecked (rough gas), Saving (rough gas) change.

A sensible order of work

  1. First make it correct and clear.
  2. Measure with a gas report to find the expensive functions.
  3. Fix the big things: storage writes, unnecessary loops and copies.
  4. Re-measure and keep only changes that pay for their complexity.
  5. Never trade away a safety check for a few gas.

Check what you just learned

1. When is unchecked arithmetic appropriate?
  • Always, to save gas
  • Never
  • For user-supplied amounts
  • Only when overflow is provably impossible (correct)

Otherwise you remove a safety net.

Check what you just learned

1. The best first step in optimising gas is to:
  • Measure where gas goes (correct)
  • Rewrite in assembly
  • Remove checks
  • Shorten names

Optimise what matters.
keyPoints: calldata, cached lengths and constants are safe wins.
unchecked is only for provably safe arithmetic.

topics.title: Measuring and deciding
topics.html:
Tools such as Hardhat's gas reporter and Foundry's gas snapshots show the gas used by each function in your tests. Use them to compare versions instead of guessing. A rule of thumb: spend effort where the gas is large and the function is called often.

Formula · Value of a gas saving

yearly value = gas saved per call × calls per year × gas price × ETH price

Saving 24,000 gas per deposit on 20,000 deposits a month at 30 gwei is 14.4 ETH a month in aggregate user savings.

Questions to ask before optimising
QuestionWhy
How often is this called?Rare functions are not worth the effort
Who pays?Users pay for every call; a small saving across thousands of users adds up
How much clarity do I lose?Unreadable code hides bugs
Can I prove the change is safe?Tests and reasoning
Will an audit be harder?Complexity costs review time

Common mistakes

  • Optimising before the code works.
  • Believing gas figures from articles instead of measuring.
  • Removing events to save gas and breaking the front end.

Check what you just learned

1. Why check gas with a report rather than guessing?
  • Reports are free
  • Intuition about gas is often wrong (correct)
  • Law requires it
  • It makes code faster

Measure, then decide.

Check what you just learned

1. A small saving is most worthwhile when the function is:
  • Never called
  • Private
  • Called very often (correct)
  • Internal only

Savings multiply.

Key terms: flip and sort

Storage slot
A 32-byte unit of persistent storage
Packing
Placing several small variables in one slot
Cold access
The first access to a slot in a transaction
calldata
Read-only input data
unchecked
A block that skips overflow checks
Gas report
A table of gas used by each function
keyPoints: Measure with gas reports and weigh value against complexity.
Optimise frequently called, expensive functions first.

modules.title: Design patterns for contracts
modules.summary: State machines, pull payments, factories and clones, and role-based access control.
modules.outcome: You can implement a state machine, pull payments, a clone factory and roles, and explain when each fits.
modules.intro: Most production contracts are combinations of a handful of well-known patterns. Knowing them by name makes your code easier to read and your reviews faster. This module shows each in a complete contract.

topics.title: State machines and pull payments: an auction
topics.html:
Patterns at work
PatternWhereWhy
State machineenum Stage and the atStage modifierFunctions only work in the right stage
Pull paymentpendingReturns and withdraw()A losing bidder who cannot receive ETH cannot block the auction
Checks-effects-interactionsstage is updated before sending ETH; pendingReturns is zeroed before the callPrevents reentrancy
Custom errorsWrongStage, TooLow and othersCheap and clear
Immutablesseller and endTimeCheap to read

Why not refund the previous bidder inside bid()? If that bidder is a contract that always rejects ETH, every later bid would revert and the auction could never move on. With pull payments, a bad actor only harms itself.

Check what you just learned

1. Why are refunds pulled rather than pushed in the Auction?
  • To save gas only
  • To hide bids
  • Because call is banned
  • So a bidder that rejects ETH cannot block the auction (correct)

A denial-of-service defence.

Check what you just learned

1. A state machine in Solidity is commonly built with:
  • An enum and a modifier (correct)
  • A library only
  • Events only
  • A string

Stage plus a check.
keyPoints: Use explicit stages to restrict functions.
Pull payments stop one bad recipient blocking everyone.

topics.title: Factories and clones
topics.html:
Deploying a full contract costs gas in proportion to its code size. When many copies are needed, such as one wallet per user, a minimal proxy (also called a clone, defined in the standard EIP-1167) is far cheaper: a tiny contract that forwards every call to a shared implementation using delegatecall. Each clone has its own storage but shares the code.

Full deployment versus a clone
New full contractMinimal proxy clone
Code stored per copyAll of itAbout 45 bytes
Deployment gasHigh and grows with code sizeLow and roughly constant
Call costDirectA little extra for the delegatecall
UpgradesEach copy is separateAll clones follow the implementation unless it is fixed (clones are not upgradeable by themselves)
InitialisationConstructorAn init function that must be protected against being called twice
Watch out

A clone has no constructor logic, so you must use an initialiser and guard it against re-initialisation, or anyone could take ownership of the wallet.

Check what you just learned

1. Why use clones for one wallet per user?
  • They are more secure by default
  • Deployment is far cheaper than full copies (correct)
  • They hide code
  • They need no initialiser

One shared implementation.

Check what you just learned

1. A clone shares with its implementation:
  • Storage
  • Owner
  • Code (correct)
  • Balance

Each has its own storage.
keyPoints: Minimal proxies share one implementation, so each copy is cheap.
Clones need a protected initialiser instead of a constructor.

topics.title: Roles instead of a single owner
topics.html:
A single owner is a single point of failure and a single target. Role-based access control splits powers: one role may spend, another may pause, another may manage roles. OpenZeppelin's AccessControl provides roles identified by a hash such as keccak256("SPENDER_ROLE"), a default admin role that can grant and revoke them, and a modifier onlyRole.

A sensible split for a treasury
RolePowerHeld by
DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLEGrant and revoke other rolesA multi-signature wallet
SPENDER_ROLEPay out approved amountsAn operations account with limits
PAUSER_ROLEStop activity in an emergencyA fast-response security account

Good practice

  • Give each role the least power it needs.
  • Keep the admin role in a multi-signature wallet.
  • Emit events when roles change (AccessControl does).
  • Document who holds each role on a public page.
  • Plan for losing or rotating a key.

Check what you just learned

1. Why separate PAUSER and ADMIN roles?
  • It costs less gas
  • The compiler requires it
  • It hides owners
  • A fast emergency stop does not need the power to move funds or change roles (correct)

Least privilege.

Check what you just learned

1. onlyRole(SPENDER_ROLE) lets:
  • Only accounts holding that role call it (correct)
  • Anyone call the function
  • Only the deployer call it
  • Nobody call it

A role check.

Key terms: flip and sort

State machine
A contract with explicit stages
Pull payment
Recipients withdraw their own funds
Minimal proxy
A tiny clone that delegates to an implementation
Factory
A contract that creates other contracts
Role
A named permission
Least privilege
Giving only the power needed
keyPoints: Roles split powers across accounts.
Keep admin power in a multi-signature wallet.

modules.title: Low-level calls and upgradeable proxies
modules.summary: call, staticcall and delegatecall, how proxies work, why storage collisions happen and how UUPS upgrades are done safely.
modules.outcome: You can explain delegatecall, spot a storage collision, write an initialiser and describe a safe upgrade process.
modules.intro: Contract code is immutable, yet products must change. Proxies resolve the contradiction: the address and data stay the same while the logic behind them is replaced. They are powerful and dangerous. This module explains how they work and how to avoid the classic mistakes.

topics.title: call, staticcall and delegatecall
topics.html:
Three low-level calls
CallWhose code runsWhose storage changesmsg.sender in the target
callThe target'sThe target'sThe calling contract
staticcallThe target'sNone (writes are forbidden)The calling contract
delegatecallThe target'sThe caller'sThe original caller (context preserved)

delegatecall is the building block of proxies. The proxy holds the data. When a user calls the proxy, the proxy delegatecalls the implementation: the implementation's code runs, but it reads and writes the proxy's storage and sees the original msg.sender and msg.value. Replace the implementation's address and the same data is now handled by new code.

Watch out

Never delegatecall to an address you do not fully control or trust. The target's code can do anything to your storage, including overwriting your owner and draining funds.

Check what you just learned

1. With delegatecall, whose storage does the executed code change?
  • The target's
  • The caller's (correct)
  • Nobody's
  • The miner's

The code is borrowed; the data stays.

Check what you just learned

1. In a delegatecall, msg.sender is:
  • The proxy
  • The implementation
  • The original caller (correct)
  • Zero

The context is preserved.
keyPoints: delegatecall runs another contract's code on your own storage.
Proxies use it to separate data from replaceable logic.

topics.title: Storage collisions
topics.html:
Because the implementation's code uses the proxy's storage, both must agree on what each slot means. If the proxy keeps its own variables, such as the implementation address, in slot 0 and the implementation also uses slot 0 for something else, the two will overwrite each other. This is a storage collision.

What goes wrong
StepEffect
User calls set(7) through the proxyThe implementation's code writes 7 to its slot 0
In the proxy, slot 0 is the implementation addressThe address is overwritten by the number 7
Next callThe proxy delegatecalls address 0x07, which has no code; the contract is bricked
How the standard avoids it
TechniqueIdea
EIP-1967 storage slotsThe proxy keeps its admin and implementation address at pseudo-random slots (derived from a hash) that normal variables never use
Inherited layoutImplementation versions only append variables and never reorder or remove them
Storage gapsReserved empty slots in base contracts so later versions can add variables
Layout checking toolsPlugins compare old and new layouts before an upgrade

Check what you just learned

1. What fixes the BrokenProxy collision in the standard design?
  • More gas
  • Making it payable
  • A longer name
  • Keeping proxy variables at special hashed slots that implementations do not use (correct)

EIP-1967 slots.

Check what you just learned

1. An upgrade that reorders state variables will:
  • Corrupt stored data (correct)
  • Be fine
  • Save gas
  • Reduce fees

Old data is read as the wrong variable.
keyPoints: Slots must mean the same thing to the proxy and the implementation.
EIP-1967 slots, append-only layouts and gaps prevent collisions.

topics.title: UUPS upgrades done carefully
topics.html:
Parts of a UUPS implementation
PiecePurpose
Initializable and initializerReplaces the constructor: runs once through the proxy to set up state
_disableInitializers() in the constructorStops anyone initialising the implementation contract itself
OwnableUpgradeableAn owner whose state lives in the proxy's storage
UUPSUpgradeable and _authorizeUpgradeThe upgrade function lives in the implementation and must be protected
BoxV2 is BoxV1A new version adds a function and keeps the old layout
UUPS compared with the transparent proxy
Transparent proxyUUPS
Where upgrade logic livesIn the proxyIn the implementation
Cost of each callSlightly higher (admin checks)Lower
RiskA bug in the proxy is hard to fixIf you forget the upgrade function in a new version, the contract can never be upgraded again

Safe upgrade rules

  1. Protect _authorizeUpgrade with strong access control, ideally a multi-signature wallet and a time-lock.
  2. Only append state variables; never reorder or remove them.
  3. Use reinitialisers with version numbers for new setup.
  4. Keep the upgrade function in every new version.
  5. Run layout-compatibility checks and rehearse on a test network and on a fork.
  6. Verify the new implementation's source before the upgrade.
Watch out

Upgradeability means the code's owner can change the rules after users have deposited. Users must trust the governance, so publish it, delay it with a time-lock and keep the power in more than one hand.

Check what you just learned

1. What does _disableInitializers() in the constructor prevent?
  • Upgrades
  • Anyone initialising the implementation contract directly (correct)
  • Fees
  • Events

The logic contract itself must stay inert.

Check what you just learned

1. If a new UUPS version omits the upgrade function:
  • Nothing happens
  • It upgrades itself
  • The contract can never be upgraded again (correct)
  • Gas is refunded

A classic mistake.

Key terms: flip and sort

delegatecall
Run another contract's code on your storage
Proxy
A contract that forwards calls to an implementation
Implementation
The logic contract behind a proxy
Storage collision
Two contracts using the same slot differently
Initialiser
A function replacing a constructor in upgradeable contracts
UUPS
A proxy pattern with upgrade logic in the implementation
keyPoints: UUPS puts upgrade logic in the implementation; guard it well.
Initialisers replace constructors; layouts only grow.

modules.title: Signatures and off-chain data
modules.summary: Verifying signatures on-chain, EIP-712 typed data, vouchers and meta-transactions, and defending against replay.
modules.outcome: You can verify a signature in Solidity, bind it against replay and explain how gasless transactions work.
modules.intro: Not everything has to be a transaction. A user can sign a message off-chain, for free, and anyone can submit it later. This powers permits, vouchers, allow-lists and gasless apps, but a signature without careful design can be reused by an attacker.

topics.title: Verifying a signature on-chain
topics.html:
What each part does
PartPurpose
keccak256(abi.encodePacked(...))Builds the digest of the data being approved
Includes address(this) and block.chainidTies the signature to one contract on one chain
Includes the nonceMakes every voucher unique
toEthSignedMessageHashApplies the standard prefix wallets add when signing text
ECDSA.recoverReturns the address that produced the signature
used[digest] = true before sendingBlocks reuse and follows checks-effects-interactions

Check what you just learned

1. Why does the voucher's digest include the contract address and chain id?
  • To save gas
  • To set fees
  • To hide data
  • So the signature cannot be replayed on another contract or chain (correct)

Replay protection.

Watch out

Use well-reviewed libraries such as OpenZeppelin's ECDSA, which also reject malleable signatures. Never write your own signature code.

Check what you just learned

1. ECDSA.recover returns:
  • The signer's address (correct)
  • The amount
  • The nonce
  • The fee

Compare it with the expected signer.
keyPoints: Recompute the digest on-chain and recover the signer.
Bind signatures to the contract, chain and a unique nonce.

topics.title: EIP-712 typed data
topics.html:
Signing a raw hash shows the user a meaningless string of hex. EIP-712 defines a way to sign structured data so that a wallet can show the user exactly what they are approving: the fields, the values and the application and chain. It also adds a domain separator binding the signature to one application, version, chain and contract.

Parts of EIP-712
PartMeaning
Domainname, version, chainId and verifyingContract: stops cross-application and cross-chain replay
Type hashA hash of the structure's definition, such as Order(address maker,uint256 amount,uint256 nonce)
Struct hashA hash of the actual values under that type
DigestThe final hash that is signed, combining a prefix, the domain and the struct hash

Why typed data is safer

  • Users can read what they sign.
  • The domain prevents reuse across apps and chains.
  • Standard libraries handle the hashing correctly.
  • Wallets can warn about suspicious requests.

Check what you just learned

1. What does the domain separator add?
  • Speed
  • Binding to one app, version, chain and contract (correct)
  • Encryption
  • A fee

Replay protection and clarity.

Check what you just learned

1. EIP-712 is mainly about:
  • Mining
  • Gas prices
  • Signing structured, readable data (correct)
  • Token supply

Safer signatures.
keyPoints: EIP-712 lets users read what they sign and binds it to a domain.
Use libraries to compute typed-data hashes.

topics.title: Replay protection and meta-transactions
topics.html:
Replay defences
DefenceBlocks
Nonce or used flagThe same signature used twice
Chain idReuse on another network
Contract addressReuse on another contract
ExpiryUse long after intended
Typed domainReuse across different applications

A meta-transaction lets a user sign an action off-chain and a relayer submit it and pay the gas. The contract checks the user's signature, then acts as if the user had called. Wallet-free sign-ups and gasless games use this. Standards such as ERC-2771 let contracts trust a designated forwarder to tell them who the real sender is.

Batching gasless actions

Change the number of actions to see the gas of sending each separately versus in batches. Teaching figures.

Adjust Actions, Gas per separate transaction, Gas per action inside a batch, Overhead per batch, Actions per batch and see Separate transactions (gas), Batched (gas) change.

Watch out

A relayer that pays gas can be abused. Limit what it will sponsor, rate-limit users and consider who pays in the long run.

Check what you just learned

1. Who pays the gas in a meta-transaction?
  • The signer
  • Nobody
  • The miner
  • A relayer who submits it (correct)

The user only signs.

Check what you just learned

1. A nonce in a signed message prevents:
  • Reuse of the same signature (correct)
  • Gas costs
  • Fees
  • Mining

Each message is single-use.

Key terms: flip and sort

ECDSA
The signature scheme used by Ethereum accounts
Digest
The hash that is signed
Nonce
A single-use number
EIP-712
A standard for signing typed data
Domain separator
Data binding a signature to one app and chain
Meta-transaction
A signed action submitted by someone else
keyPoints: Nonces, chain id, contract address, expiry and domain stop replay.
Meta-transactions let a relayer pay gas for signed actions.

modules.title: Advanced testing
modules.summary: Unit, fuzz, invariant, fork and integration tests, and how to choose among them.
modules.outcome: You can choose the right kind of test, write invariants for a contract and read a fuzzing example.
modules.intro: A handful of hand-written examples proves little about contracts that handle money in unforeseeable ways. Professional teams add randomised and stateful testing that explores the situations nobody thought of.

topics.title: A map of test types
topics.html:
Test types
TypeWhat it doesFinds
Unit testChecks one behaviour with chosen inputsLogic errors in a single function
Fuzz testThe tool generates many random inputs for a functionEdge cases and arithmetic problems
Invariant testThe tool calls random sequences of functions and checks properties that must always holdBroken accounting, stage violations, unexpected interactions
Fork testRuns against a copy of real network stateProblems with real dependencies such as real tokens
Integration testSeveral contracts working togetherWiring and permission mistakes

In the example, the fuzzer supplies a, b and c, and the test asserts that both sum functions give the same answer for all of them. If any random case disagreed, the tool would report the exact failing input and let you replay it.

Check what you just learned

1. Which test explores random sequences of calls to check a property?
  • Unit test
  • Invariant test (correct)
  • Fork test
  • Integration test

Stateful property testing.

Tip

Fuzzing is cheap to start: turn function arguments into test parameters and add bounds so that inputs are meaningful.

Check what you just learned

1. A fork test is useful because it:
  • Is faster
  • Needs no code
  • Uses a copy of real network state (correct)
  • Hides bugs

Realistic dependencies.
keyPoints: Unit, fuzz, invariant, fork and integration tests each find different bugs.
Fuzzers report the exact failing input.

topics.title: Thinking in invariants
topics.html:
Definition

Invariant. A property that must be true at all times, whatever sequence of actions has happened. Examples: the contract holds enough ETH to cover what it owes; a token's total supply equals the sum of balances; a state machine never moves backwards.

Invariants for the Auction
InvariantMeaning
Solvencycontract balance ≥ sum of pending returns + current highest bid (while open)
Monotonic bidhighestBid never decreases
Forward-only stagestage never returns from Ended to Open
One payoutthe seller is paid exactly once
No double withdrawalafter a withdrawal, the user's pending return is zero

How to find invariants

  1. Ask what must never happen.
  2. Ask what quantity should always add up.
  3. Look at every state variable and ask what relationship it has with others.
  4. Write the property as a function that returns true or false.
  5. Let the tool call random functions and check it after each call.

Check what you just learned

1. Which is a good invariant for a token?
  • The price is high
  • The name is short
  • Gas is low
  • The total supply equals the sum of all balances (correct)

A conservation property.

Watch out

An invariant test is only as good as its properties and its handlers. Weak or missing properties give false confidence.

Check what you just learned

1. A solvency invariant says:
  • The contract can always pay what it owes (correct)
  • The contract owes nothing
  • The contract is cheap
  • The contract is public

Assets cover liabilities.
keyPoints: Invariants are properties that must always hold.
Look for conservation, ordering and forward-only rules.

topics.title: Coverage, mutation and review
topics.html:
Other quality tools
ToolWhat it tells you
Coverage reportWhich lines and branches your tests ran; unrun code is untested code
Mutation testingSmall deliberate changes to the code (mutants); if tests still pass, they are weak
Static analysisAutomated scans for known bug patterns
Formal verificationMathematical proof of selected properties (specialised)
Code reviewHumans reading the code against the specification
Independent auditExperienced reviewers examining design and code

High coverage does not prove correctness, but low coverage proves the opposite: some code was never exercised. Use coverage to find gaps, then think about what each gap could hide.

A layered approach

  • Write unit tests as you code.
  • Add fuzz tests for arithmetic and parsing.
  • Add invariants for accounting and state.
  • Run static analysis in continuous integration.
  • Review in pairs and prepare a threat model.
  • Commission an audit for anything holding real value.

Check what you just learned

1. What does a mutation that survives (tests still pass) tell you?
  • The code is perfect
  • Your tests did not notice a change in behaviour (correct)
  • The compiler is broken
  • Gas is low

The tests are weak there.

Check what you just learned

1. High coverage proves:
  • Correctness
  • Security
  • Nothing by itself about correctness (correct)
  • Low gas

It shows what ran, not what was checked.

Key terms: flip and sort

Fuzzing
Testing with many random inputs
Invariant
A property that must always hold
Fork test
A test against copied real network state
Coverage
How much code the tests execute
Mutation testing
Checking that tests catch small code changes
Static analysis
Automated scanning for bug patterns
keyPoints: Coverage finds untested code; mutation testing finds weak tests.
Layer tests, tools, review and audit.

modules.title: Production practice
modules.summary: Documentation, threat modelling, audit preparation and the discipline of safe releases.
modules.outcome: You can document contracts with NatSpec, threat-model a design, prepare for an audit and run a safe release.
modules.intro: Code that holds other people's money needs more than correctness: it needs documentation, a threat model, a release process and a plan for when things go wrong. This module covers the habits of teams who ship contracts for a living.

topics.title: Documentation that helps reviewers
topics.html:
NatSpec tags
TagUse
@title, @authorDescribe the contract
@noticePlain-language description for users, shown by wallets and explorers
@devNotes for developers: assumptions and warnings
@paramWhat each input means
@returnWhat the function returns
@custom:...Project-specific tags, such as security contacts

What good documentation includes

  1. A one-page specification that says what the system must do and what it must never do.
  2. NatSpec on every external function.
  3. A list of roles and what each can do.
  4. A diagram of contracts and how they call each other.
  5. A list of trust assumptions: oracles, admins and external contracts.
  6. A known issues list.
Tip

If an auditor has to guess what you meant, they will spend your money on guessing. Clear documentation makes reviews faster, cheaper and better.

Check what you just learned

1. Which tag describes a function for end users in wallets and explorers?
  • @dev
  • @custom
  • @param
  • @notice (correct)

@notice is user-facing.

Check what you just learned

1. @param documents:
  • Each input (correct)
  • The licence
  • The gas
  • The owner

One line per parameter.
keyPoints: Use NatSpec, a specification and a trust-assumption list.
Clear documentation makes audits faster.

topics.title: Threat modelling and audit preparation
topics.html:
Common threat questions
QuestionExample
What if this external call re-enters?Reentrancy on withdraw
What if this admin key is stolen?Role compromise and time-lock
What if this oracle is wrong or late?Price manipulation
What if this input is extreme?Zero, maximum, very long arrays
What if the order of transactions changes?Front-running and sandwiching
What if gas costs rise or a loop grows?Denial of service
What if an upgrade breaks storage?Layout corruption

Preparing for an audit

  • Freeze the code and tag the version.
  • Provide the specification, diagrams and test instructions.
  • Make sure tests pass and coverage is high.
  • Run static analysis and fix the easy findings first.
  • Explain the assumptions and the areas you are least sure about.
  • Reserve time to fix findings and have them re-checked.

Check what you just learned

1. What is a residual risk?
  • A fixed bug
  • A risk that remains after mitigations (correct)
  • A type of fee
  • A role

Record what you could not remove.

Check what you just learned

1. Before an audit you should:
  • Keep changing the code
  • Remove tests
  • Freeze the version and supply documentation (correct)
  • Hide risks

Auditors need a stable target.
keyPoints: Threat modelling lists assets, actors, entry points and what could go wrong.
Prepare an audit with a frozen version, documents and tests.

topics.title: Release and incident discipline
topics.html:
A release process
StageChecks
PrepareTests green, audit findings fixed, version tagged
RehearseDeploy to a test network and to a fork; run the full upgrade or launch script
AnnouncePublish the verified source, addresses and a change summary
Launch graduallyDeposit caps, allow-lists or a small first phase
MonitorAlerts on large transfers, role changes, pauses and unusual calls
RespondA written incident plan: who pauses, who communicates, who investigates

Why start with a cap

Change the cap and the chance of a serious bug to see the expected loss. A teaching model with made-up numbers.

Adjust Deposit cap (rupees), Chance of a serious bug (%) and see Expected loss if bugs are exploited fully (rupees) change.

When something goes wrong

  1. Pause if you can. Stop the loss first.
  2. Tell users clearly and quickly what you know and do not know.
  3. Preserve the evidence: transactions, logs and code versions.
  4. Fix, test and rehearse the fix before applying it.
  5. Publish a post-mortem: what happened, why and what will change.
Watch out

This course teaches concepts and habits. It does not make a contract safe. Real deployments need professional audits, legal advice and continuing operations.

Check what you just learned

1. Why launch with deposit caps?
  • To look small
  • To avoid events
  • To save gas
  • To limit the harm if an undiscovered bug exists (correct)

A cap limits the blast radius.

Check what you just learned

1. After an incident you should publish:
  • A post-mortem (correct)
  • Nothing
  • A new token
  • A fee

Trust grows from honesty.

Key terms: flip and sort

NatSpec
Structured documentation comments in Solidity
Threat model
A structured list of what could go wrong
Residual risk
A risk that remains after mitigation
Audit
An independent security review
Deposit cap
A limit on funds a contract may hold
Post-mortem
A written account of an incident
keyPoints: Prepare, rehearse, announce, launch gradually, monitor and respond.
Pause first, communicate honestly, then fix and learn.
